analysis.one_liner: Writes EPA's 2001 arsenic-in-drinking-water safety limit (10 parts per billion) into federal law.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 173 cosponsors but died in committee without a single hearing or vote; the arsenic standard it defended took effect anyway in 2001-2002.
analysis.plain_summary: In January 2001, EPA finalized a rule tightening the arsenic limit in drinking water from 50 to 10 parts per billion. The new administration suspended the rule pending review, so this bill would have written the standard directly into law, making it untouchable by regulatory delay, and doubled federal funding to help water systems pay for compliance. The bill never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose drinking water comes from systems with elevated natural arsenic, mostly in the West, Midwest, and parts of New England. EPA estimated the 10 ppb standard would cut arsenic exposure for millions of Americans and reduce cancer risk. The bill also would have doubled the federal fund that helps local water systems afford treatment upgrades.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the January 22, 2001 EPA rule — an enforceable arsenic limit of 0.010 mg/L (10 micrograms per liter) plus a health-based goal — have the force and effect of law, so it cannot be delayed or withdrawn by the administration.
Doubles authorization for the Safe Drinking Water Act's state revolving fund from $1 billion to $2 billion, the main federal source of money helping local water systems pay for arsenic treatment.
Includes a savings clause leaving EPA's authority to revisit the standard intact, and grew to 173 cosponsors including the House Democratic leadership.

analysis.who_pays: Water utilities — especially small systems serving fewer than 10,000 people in areas with naturally high arsenic — would bear the cost of new treatment, and federal taxpayers would fund the doubled $2 billion aid program. Those costs would eventually show up in water rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Small water systems and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small water systems; EPA and Congress estimated the 10 ppb standard would cost hundreds of millions of dollars a year, which is why the bill pairs the standard with a doubled federal aid fund rather than absorbing the cost alone.
Doubling the revolving-fund authorization to $2 billion is new federal spending that would add to the deficit unless offset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit — a legally enforceable arsenic limit ten times stricter than the old 50 ppb standard, with federal money to ease the burden — substantially outweighs the compliance costs, which the bill itself addresses by doubling aid. The honest objection is that small systems face real, concentrated costs even with help.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Waxman introduced the bill on April 4, 2001, two months after EPA published the 10 ppb arsenic rule in the final days of the previous administration.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on April 4, and on April 16 to the Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials — its last official action.
173 House members cosponsored it — 171 of 208 House Democrats, the chamber's one Independent, and a single Republican — but the committee never held a hearing or vote before the 107th Congress ended.

In practice the bill's core goal was achieved another way: the administration review ended with EPA reaffirming the 10 ppb standard in 2001, and the rule took effect with compliance deadlines in 2006.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drinking-water customers ultimately got the arsenic standard anyway, because EPA went forward with the rule it had suspended, so the bill's death cost the public little. Water systems and the industries that had sought delay gained a few months of breathing room in 2001, and the standard never gained the extra permanence the bill would have given it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water customers, once EPA adopted the rule anyway

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), bill sponsor and ranking member on the committee's environment panel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 172 cosponsors in a single day to lock the arsenic rule into law.

for.name: 173 of 208 House Democrats plus the chamber's one Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Democratic leader Gephardt and senior committee members.

for.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 4, 2001 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Water utilities and mining interests
against.role: Opponents of the stricter arsenic standard
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the 10 ppb standard during EPA's rulemaking and the 2001 review, citing compliance costs for small systems.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was overwhelmingly Democratic: 171 of 208 House Democrats signed on, versus exactly 1 of 223 Republicans, and it died in a Republican-controlled committee without a hearing.

industries.industry: Water utilities, especially small community systems
industries.note: The rule forces treatment upgrades costing hundreds of millions of dollars a year, hitting small systems hardest. Utilities' interest in the old 50 ppb standard ran against customers' interest in lower arsenic exposure, though the bill's doubled federal fund partially offsets the cost.

industries.industry: Mining and other industries whose waste contributes arsenic to water sources
industries.note: A stricter drinking-water standard tightens pressure on upstream sources of arsenic contamination and can raise their waste-treatment obligations.

industries.industry: Water treatment technology and engineering firms
industries.note: Mandating the 10 ppb standard creates a market for arsenic-removal equipment, and the doubled $2 billion revolving fund pays systems to buy it.
